reasons: Errors are caught and logged in a consistent way.
No test is visible for these endpoints or the startup behavior.
Cross-origin access is open to all origins.
Auto-reload is on by default, which is a development setting.

terms.meaning: A Python framework for building web services that other programs or pages call.
A web address the app answers, such as /health.
A group of related endpoints that is attached to the app under a shared path.
Code that runs once when the app starts and once when it stops.
A browser rule about which web pages may call this server. Allowing all origins makes it open to any site.
A simple endpoint that reports whether the service is working, for monitoring tools or people.
The server program that actually listens for web requests and runs the app.
Log lines written as machine-readable data, usually JSON, so they can be searched.

depends_on: routes package (projects, research, normalization, capex, schedule, exports)
used_by: Started by uvicorn with the target main:app
Run directly as a script for development

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and logging setup
sections.what: Loads the web framework, database helpers, and route modules, then sets logs to a JSON line format.
sections.why: Logs in one machine-readable format make them easier to search later.
sections.watch_out: Route modules are imported here, so a broken import in any one of them stops the whole app from starting.

sections.name: lifespan (part 1)
sections.title: Startup and shutdown steps
sections.what: On startup, checks the database, builds missing tables, and stops with an error if the database cannot be reached. On shutdown, writes a log line.
sections.why: Prevents the app from serving requests with no working database, and prepares tables before the first request.
sections.watch_out: A failing database stops startup, so check database settings before debugging the app itself.

sections.name: lifespan (part 2)
sections.title: Cross-origin access setting
sections.what: Lets web pages from any address call this API from a browser, including pages opened as local files.
sections.why: The code comment says this is for local development so a frontend can open from file paths.
sections.watch_out: Allowing every origin is risky on a shared or production server, because any website can call the API from a visitor's browser.

sections.name: value_error_handler
sections.title: Turns bad input errors into 400 responses
sections.what: When code raises a ValueError, the caller receives a 400 Bad Request response with the error message, instead of a crash.
sections.why: Likely reason: gives callers a clear reply when they send bad input. No further reason is stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The error message is sent back to the caller, so avoid putting private details into ValueError messages.

sections.name: general_exception_handler
sections.title: Catches all other errors safely
sections.what: For any other unhandled error, logs the full details and returns a generic 500 message, so internal details are not shown to callers.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps crash details out of responses while still recording them for the team.
sections.watch_out: Callers only see a generic message, so someone must read the logs to find the cause of a 500 error.

sections.name: health_check
sections.title: Health check endpoint
sections.what: Answers at /health with whether the database is reachable, the database type, and the version number. This block also attaches six route groups under /api/v1.
sections.why: Lets monitoring tools or people check status without logging in. The router attachment is grouped here in the file.
sections.watch_out: Each health call runs a database test, so frequent polling adds load.

sections.name: root
sections.title: Root information endpoint
sections.what: Answers at / with the app name, version, a short description, and links to the docs and health endpoints.
sections.why: Gives a simple landing response so a visitor can find the documentation.
sections.watch_out: The version 1.0.0 is written in several places in this file, so update every copy when releasing.

sections.name: entry point
sections.title: Direct start of the server
sections.what: When the file is run directly, starts the web server on the host and port from settings, with auto-reload on by default.
sections.why: Lets a developer start the app with one command without typing server options.
sections.watch_out: Auto-reload is on by default, which suits development but should be turned off on a shared server.

summary: Starts the web application, checks the database on startup, sets up error responses, and provides the health and root endpoints.
purpose: The entry point for the whole platform. It attaches the route groups for projects, research, normalization, capex, schedule, and exports under their own web paths.
why: Likely reason: one place that builds the app and connects its parts. The reason for open cross-origin access is not fully stated, though a comment says it is for local development.
how: 1. Configures structured JSON logging. 2. Creates the FastAPI app with a title and description. 3. On startup, the lifespan function tests the database, builds missing tables, and refuses to start if the connection fails. 4. Allows cross-origin requests from any site. 5. Registers handlers for ValueError and for any other error. 6. Adds the health and root endpoints. 7. Attaches six route groups under /api/v1 paths. 8. If the file is run directly, starts the server with host, port and reload settings.
inputs: Environment settings API_HOST, API_PORT and RELOAD. Functions and flags from the database module. Route modules. Incoming web requests.
outputs: A running web server. JSON responses for health, root and errors. Structured log lines. Interactive API documentation at /docs and /redoc.
risks: Open cross-origin access lets any website call the API from a browser. Auto-reload is on by default. If the database is down, the app will not start. No login check is visible in this file, so protection must live elsewhere.
debug: If the app will not start, read database_connection_failed or database_connection_test log lines first. If a request returns a 500 error, search logs for unhandled_exception, which includes the full trace. Visit /health to see whether the database is reachable. If a route is missing, check its import in the routes package.
